digital_history.description: Historical inquiry using digital media to assemble and interpret evidence, develop arguments, publish scholarship, teach and involve public audiences. Digital history overlaps with quantitative history, public history and digital humanities without being equivalent to any of them.

liberal_order_framework.label: Liberal order framework
liberal_order_framework.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · selected later readings
liberal_order_framework.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures. Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
liberal_order_framework.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).
liberal_order_framework.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics; Bannister proposes a loyalist order for 1750–1840 (chapter title), its relation to McKay not characterized. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.

cdn_sixties.label: Canada’s 1960s
cdn_sixties.date_label: Early accounts: Kostash 1980, Levitt 1984 · Behiels 1985 · Owram 1996 · Igartua 2006 · Palmer, Warren 2008–09 · Mills 2010 · Debating Dissent 2012 · selected later readings
cdn_sixties.description: Historical writing that treats Canada's long 1960s as a subject in its own right: the baby boom and youth revolt, the New Left and labour militancy, Quebec's Quiet Revolution and its radicalisms, rights movements, decolonization and Red Power, and the remaking of national identity. Early book-length accounts include Kostash's interview-based history of her own generation (1980) and Levitt (1984). Doug Owram's Born at the Right Time (1996) followed the baby-boom generation from suburb and school to counterculture and youth radicalism. José Igartua's The Other Quiet Revolution (2006) traced English Canada's British self-definition giving way to a civic, rights-based identity, and Dominique Clément studied its rights associations. Bryan Palmer's Canada's 1960s (2009) read the decade through the ironies of national identity, with chapters on wildcat strikes, the New Left, Quebec and the 'discovery' of the 'Indian'. Sean Mills's The Empire Within (2010) traced postcolonial thought in Montreal activism, and David Austin race, sex and security there. Campbell, Clément and Kealey's Debating Dissent (2012) and Ian Milligan's Rebel Youth (2014), on young workers and New Leftists, widened the field. Francophone historians debate continuity and rupture. Michael Behiels, E.-Martin Meunier and Jean-Philippe Warren, and Louise Bienvenue found the Quiet Revolution's roots in postwar liberalism and in Catholic Action, against its own story of a 'grande noirceur'. Warren's Une douce anarchie (2008) historicized the student revolt of 1968. It is a recent synthesis literature resting on a few reference works (Owram, Palmer, Mills, Igartua), not a school like the atlas's New Left entry.

Comparison: Marwick, The Sixties (1998).
cdn_sixties.scope_note: A research field defined by its subject, the long 1960s (roughly late 1950s to early 1970s), not by a method or school. It replaces the "postwar Canada" data cluster (user, 2026-10-12: "1960s is its own thing"). Distinguish the atlas's New Left entry (radical historians as a school) from histories of the New Left as a movement. The Quebec strand overlaps Quebec historiography and the Catholic Action revision in religion history; those works remain treated mainly there. Black Canadian sixties history: Austin (2013) is a later reading; before 2000 the only verified work is a contemporary participants' collection (Forsythe, ed., 1971), so pre-2000 scholarly coverage is a gap.

settler_colonialism.label: Settler colonialism
settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999 · selected later readings: Wolfe 2006, Veracini 2010, journal 2011, critiques 2013–20; field chronology unresolved
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
settler_colonialism.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) and “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. settler_colonialism.scope_note: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.

languages_of_class.label: The languages of class debate
languages_of_class.date_label: The Making 1963 · Languages of Class 1983 · ILWCH forum 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · Visions of the People 1991 · Vernon 1994 · “The End of Social History?” 1995 · Speaking for the People 1998 · ILWCH 57 2000 · The Future of Class in History 2007
languages_of_class.description: Linked disputes over how experience, language, gender and social relations shape class formation and historical explanation. Thompson's preface (1963) made class a relationship, not a thing; Stedman Jones's Languages of Class (1983) set 'the linguistic cat among the social history pigeons' (Eley and Nield's words), while holding that 'how the two relate' — social and linguistic — 'must be rethought' (as quoted by Epstein). Foster, Gray, Epstein and Kirk answered (1985–87); Joan Scott asked that language and gender be taken seriously; Bryan Palmer replied (1987–90). Patrick Joyce set a 'family of populisms' against class (1991) and asked 'The End of Social History?' (1995); James Vernon asked who was afraid of the linguistic turn (1994); Jon Lawrence combined 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches (1998). Related and intersecting controversies developed across several regions: Rancière and Sewell in France, Wilentz and Katznelson in the US, Canning in Germany, Chakrabarty and Chandavarkar in India, James in Latin America, Cooper in Africa, Parr and Sangster in Canada. Eley and Nield asked for 'a truce in the Left's culture wars' (Cooper, 2000) and wrote its retrospective (2007).

strands.title: From experience to language: Thompson's preface to Languages of Class, 1963–83
strands.focus: Linked disputes over how experience, language and social relations shape class formation ran through the 1970s before the linguistic turn. Thompson's preface (1963) made class a historical relationship rather than a thing (the wording is on edge_924); Eley and Nield recalled 'the inspiration of Edward Thompson and Sheila Rowbotham' (2000, p. 24) and Cooper that Thompson 'wanted to show how the working class made itself, but never doubted that what was made was the working class' (2000, n. 11). From inside Marxism, Richard Johnson's 'Edward Thompson, Eugene Genovese, and Socialist-Humanist History' (1978) named a new 'culturalism', a word Eley and Nield recall adopting in 1980 (2007, preface); the Ruskin History Workshop of December 1979 was 'brought to a head' by The Poverty of Theory (Eley and Nield 2000, n. 46); Perry Anderson's Arguments within English Marxism (1980) found 'a disconcerting lack of objective coordinates as the narrative of class formation unfolds' (p. 33, as quoted by Bergquist 1990). Stedman Jones's 'The Language of Chartism' appeared in 1982 in The Chartist Experience, edited by Epstein and Dorothy Thompson, and in extended form as 'Rethinking Chartism' in Languages of Class (1983). The introduction set the programme: historians had set fragments of speech 'into direct relation to a putative experiential reality' (p. 21, as quoted by Foster); they should instead 'study the production of interest, identification, grievance and aspiration within political languages themselves' (p. 22, as quoted by Foster), without any 'simple prejudgement about the determining role of the "social"' (p. 7, as quoted by Epstein). Radicalism was 'a vocabulary of political exclusion' (p. 104, as quoted by Foster and Epstein), not the ideology of a class. He did not propose to replace a social interpretation with a linguistic one: 'rather it is how the two relate, that must be rethought' (p. 95, as quoted by Epstein, p. 202). He placed himself after Thompson, whose 'great achievement' had freed class consciousness from economic reduction, while rejecting the 'relatively direct relationship' Thompson assumed between social being and consciousness (p. 101, as quoted by Foster).

strands.title: The first critics, 1985–87: from Foster to the ILWCH forum
strands.focus: The answers came from labour historians who accepted the attack on economic reductionism and refused its conclusion. John Foster (New Left Review, 1985), whose own Oldham study Stedman Jones had reviewed in 1975, called the theory 'undeveloped', set Volosinov's 'multi-accentuality' against Saussure, and read the book as 'an intellectual declassing of our understanding of language'. Robert Gray (Social History, 1986) found post-structuralist work on language 'a field of debate' rather than a method (p. 367, as quoted by Kirk). James Epstein (Labour/Le Travail, 1986) praised 'the most sustained and coherent descriptive analysis yet of formal Chartist ideology' but held that a public political language excludes symbolic action and that the fight over 'the people' was itself 'a form of class struggle'. Neville Kirk (IRSH, 1987) gave 'full support' to the opposition to reductionism and concluded that language and politics had been 'wrenched loose from their material determinations': 'an unconvincing idealism'. In International Labor and Working-Class History (1987) Joan Scott answered from the other side: labour historians 'reduce this important concept [language] to the study of "words"' (p. 1), and Stedman Jones had used theories of language 'in an essentially conservative manner' (as the journal's editors summarised her). Bryan Palmer answered her from the Halifax strikes of 1842, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism"' (p. 14); Christine Stansell sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss' (p. 24); Anson Rabinbach held that in Stedman Jones language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott's reply: 'class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (pp. 40–41). Cronin (1986) and Ellen Wood (1986) belong here but are unread.

strands.title: Visions of the people: populism against class, 1991–94
strands.focus: Joyce's Visions of the People (1991) held that 'the fixation with class' had denied historians 'sight of these other visions of the social order' in industrial England; its 'controlling narrative' concerned 'a righteous and dispossessed "people"' in a 'family of populisms', and popular Liberalism was 'about the union of the classes against class' (pp. 1, 56 ff., 329). Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) made popular constitutionalism the master narrative and found identities 'not done justice by Patrick Joyce's "family of populisms"' (p. 297, as quoted by Tilly); 'the invention of democracy in England was then a sham' (p. 336, as quoted by Tilly). Cannadine's review (NYRB, 1992; unread) asked, in Joyce's report of it, for 'a history of status', and his reply to Joyce's letter caricatured Joyce as reducing status to rhetoric and rejecting class as a grand concept (1993); Joyce answered that populism's flexibility enabled a history of social unities and differences. Tilly found in both 'softcore solipsism' by historians who 'remain captives of Thompson' (1994); Lawrence asked 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994); Kirk gave 'a materialist view' (1994); Vernon asked 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994; unread). Democratic Subjects (1994) carried Joyce's reading of class to narrative and the self.

strands.title: The new political history, 1993–99
strands.focus: The Social History round on Stedman Jones (Mayfield and Thorne, 1992; Lawrence and Taylor's reply and Joyce's note, 1993; Mayfield and Thorne's reply, 1993; all unread beyond the 1992 abstract) passed into a new political history. Vernon's Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives in the political history of England's long nineteenth century'; Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' and the assumption of 'an increasing class-based electorate' (both as quoted by LoPatin); Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party', reconsidering the 'homogeneity' of the working class claimed by Hobsbawm and by Savage and Miles, and relocating popular politics in place and gender. Vernon reviewed it as 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed', written 'as though … by a schizophrenic' (1999); Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined and that scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'. Cannadine's Class in Britain (1998) offered three vernacular 'models' of class instead (as Willetts reports). The field strand political/new_political_history keeps each author's contribution.

strands.title: Gender, race and the making of class, 1986–2000
strands.focus: Eley and Nield dated gender's entry into ILWCH's field of vision to Scott's 1987 controversy (2000, p. 4); the debate developed alongside wider feminist revisions of class history. Carolyn Steedman's Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) set 'two working-class childhoods' in 'history, politics, psychoanalysis and feminism' (publisher description); Sonya Rose's Limited Livelihoods (1992) made gender pivotal in 'the massive reorganization of lives and livelihoods that accompanied industrial capitalism' (publisher description); Catherine Hall's White, Male and Middle Class (1992; metadata) and Anna Clark's The Struggle for the Breeches (1995) followed; Eley and Nield judged that 'the study of class has benefited powerfully from feminist revisions' (2000, p. 8). In Germany Canning, in Canada Parr and Sangster, in Latin America French and James (1997) carried gender into the class question (see the regional strands). David Roediger's The Wages of Whiteness (1991) asked how 'race and class came together' in the antebellum United States, treating white working-class racism as 'psychological and ideological' rather than only economic (publisher description); Cooper noted how wage earners could 'make claims in terms of a white working class, indeed a white, male working class' (2000, n. 10). Scott objected in 2000 that Eley and Nield spoke of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70).

strands.title: Farewell to the working class? Retrospects and new bearings, 2000–16
strands.focus: In 2000 Eley and Nield asked 'Farewell to the Working Class?' Scott answered that they 'foreclose other possibilities' and quipped 'Assent to Discourse' (p. 69); Cooper that their piece read 'like a plea for E. P. Thompson and Joan Scott to sit down together' but 'they did not think to ask Karl Marx' (p. 61). The Future of Class in History (2007) sought 'collaborative conversation across the polarized differences between social and cultural historians' (preface, p. vii). Joyce's ego-histoire related his 'interest in "the social"' to 'Irish and class identity' (2001); The Social in Question (2002) printed Latour's case for 'association' in place of 'the social'; The Rule of Freedom (2003) and The State of Freedom (2013) took Foucauldian governmentality and 'the new materialism' into the city and the state. In 'What Is the Social in Social History?' (2010) Joyce judged the 1990s debate partly 'vigorous and unproductive': 'heat exceeded light'. Gunn and Vernon's Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity (2011), from the conference for Joyce's retirement, returned to the Thompson–Anderson 'peculiarities' debate 'viewed through a "history of classes"'; Lawrence there argued for a 'conservative' modernity, and with Feldman recalled social history's 'retreat … as a "totalising" project'. strands.title: The United States: class formation and exceptionalism, 1984–93
strands.focus: The American round began three years before Scott's, in the same journal. Sean Wilentz argued, in the editors' summary, that 'the Euro-centric concept of a mass-based socialist or communist party as the appropriate index of class consciousness diverts attention from the ways in which workers in the United States have battled the system of wage labor' (ILWCH 26, 1984, p. v); Nick Salvatore replied that one must 'use carefully three related but quite different terms: class consciousness, class conflict and class formation' and that Wilentz had not 'travelled as far as he would wish from the position outlined by Louis Hartz' (pp. 26, 28); Michael Hanagan held that embedding in a country's political structure makes a difference (editors' remarks). Ira Katznelson and Aristide Zolberg's Working-Class Formation (1986) asked 'how class, rather than other social bonds, became central' to working people's 'ideologies, dispositions, and actions' across France, Germany and the United States, with chapters by Sewell, Perrot, Cottereau, Bridges, Shefter, Kocka and Nolan (publisher description); Eley and Nield note that it 'missed gender entirely' (2000, p. 4). Berlanstein's Rethinking Labor History (1993) carried Sewell's 'post-materialist rhetoric for labor history' (as cited by Sangster), answered in Frader's 'Dissent over Discourse' (1995; both unread).
strands.works: Wilentz, 'Against Exceptionalism', with Salvatore and Hanagan (ILWCH 26, 1984); Katznelson and Zolberg, eds, Working-Class Formation (1986); Berlanstein, ed., Rethinking Labor History (1993); Frader, 'Dissent over Discourse' (1995)

strands.title: Canada: materialist feminism and the discursive turn, 1990–2000
strands.focus: In Canada the debate arrived through Labour/Le Travail. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) held that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (p. xiii, as quoted by Callinicos 1992; the publisher: 'language is not life'); Mariana Valverde asked whether Scott 'exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make' (1990, p. 233); Joy Parr's The Gender of Breadwinners (1990) and 'Gender History and Historical Practice' (1995) deconstructed skill while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (Sangster 2000, p. 157). Joan Sangster's survey (2000) set 'the post-structuralist subject' against 'the Thompsonian subject whose consciousness emerged from the interplay of human agency with social, cultural and economic formations' (p. 158), set the Canadian feminists' retained 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' against 'the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott', and objected that when 'international writers' — Sewell, in Berlanstein's volume — suggest the economy is 'simply "constructed as material" (I'm sure the unemployed feel differently!), a more fundamental boundary is violated' (p. 157), tied 'the academic retreat from class' to 'the decline of the political and intellectual left' (p. 154), and concluded that 'easy accommodation, resting comfortably under one umbrella, is not possible' (p. 161). Tilly's 'Softcore Solipsism' (1994) appeared in the same journal. The existing strand cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000 covers the same ground from the Canadian field's side.
strands.works: Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Valverde (1990; 1995); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), 'Gender History and Historical Practice' (1995); Tilly (1994); Sangster, 'Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History' (2000); see cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000

strands.title: France: the language of labor and the myth of the artisan, 1980–89
strands.focus: William Sewell's Work and Revolution in France (1980) treated 'the "language of labor" in the broadest sense' and argued that 'The nineteenth-century labor movement was born in the craft workshop, not in the dark, satanic mill' (ch. 1 opening), with 1830 as 'the emergence of class consciousness' (ch. 9 title). Jacques Rancière's 'The Myth of the Artisan' (1983), the journal's first scholarly controversy, held that the skilled artisan's 'culture as a seminal force in the development of the working-class and socialist movement is exaggerated and stems from later internal myth-making' (editors' remarks); answered by Sewell and Christopher Johnson, he replied that 'the point at stake is the democratic meaning of worker militancy', that militants 'were sons of the French Revolution rather than of corporative struggle; Julien Sorel's brothers rather than Poor Richard's', and that social history 'in its new "cultural" approach, rests on a far too restrictive understanding of "social" struggle' (1984, pp. 42, 44, 45). William Reddy's Money and Liberty in Modern Europe (1987) found 'an increasingly poor fit' between class concepts 'and the reality they purport to explain' and proposed a new concept of exchange and authority (publisher description). Scott's 1988 chapter on Sewell is unread; in 2000 she returned to Rancière as 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield'.
strands.works: Sewell, Work and Revolution in France (1980); Rancière, 'The Myth of the Artisan' (ILWCH 24, 1983), with Sewell's and Johnson's responses, and 'A Reply' (1984); Reddy, The Rise of Market Culture (1984), Money and Liberty in Modern Europe (1987); Scott, Gender and the Politics of History (1988), ch. 5

strands.title: Germany: gender and the politics of class formation, 1989–97
strands.focus: German labour history met the debate through Alltagsgeschichte and gender. Geoff Eley's 'Labor History, Social History, Alltagsgeschichte' (JMH 1989), Alf Lüdtke's Eigen-Sinn (1993) and Jürgen Kocka's class-formation studies (Lohnarbeit und Klassenbildung, 1983; 'Traditionsbindung und Klassenbildung', 1986) are placed here by title and metadata only: none was read, and no argument is attributed to them. Kathleen Canning's 'Gender and the Politics of Class Formation' (AHR 1992; unread) and Languages of Labor and Gender (1996; contents read) 'disengaged class from the sovereignty of "objective" economic and social interests' while remaining 'Grounded in imaginative and meticulous studies of labor markets, workplace organization, job cultures, family and household dynamics' (Eley and Nield 2000, p. 8); a German reviewer saw it bringing 'poststrukturalistische Überlegungen zur Bedeutung von Sprache' into dialogue with structural history (Küster 2005). Stedman Jones restated his position in a Göttingen volume edited by Lüdtke (1997; unread; Eley and Nield n. 18, 20).
strands.works: Kocka (1983; 1986); Eley, JMH 61 (1989); Canning, AHR 97 (1992), 'The Man Transformed into a Maiden?' (ILWCH 49, 1996), Languages of Labor and Gender (1996); Lüdtke, Eigen-Sinn (1993); Stedman Jones in Lüdtke, ed. (1997); Welskopp (1998); Küster (2005)

strands.title: South Asia, Africa and Latin America: experience, culture and the colonial working class, 1988–2000
strands.focus: Eley and Nield wrote that their discussion 'could easily be carried into African, Latin-American, and South Asian contexts' (2000, n. 2). Dipesh Chakrabarty's Rethinking Working-Class History (1989) read Bengal's jute workers against 'an assumption regarding "culture" built into Marx's category of "capital"' and declared 'Culture, one might say, is the "unthought" of Indian Marxism' (pp. xi–xii; edge_916), separating his argument from Thompson's (p. 5 n. 9). Rajnarayan Chandavarkar's The Origins of Industrial Capitalism in India (1994) argued that both capital and labour were internally fragmented (publisher description); his 1997 essay examined Thompson and Indian history; its previously recorded quotations await re-verification. Imperial Power and Popular Politics (1998) 'reasserts the critical role of the working classes' (publisher description) and was reviewed by Chakrabarty (AHR 1999; unread). The ILWCH controversy of 1989 was Emilia Viotti da Costa's 'Experience versus Structures', citing Thompson's Ruskin paper and Scott's 1987 essay (reference list), with Barbara Weinstein replying 'What We Gain'. Daniel James's Resistance and Integration (1988) tried 'to avoid what the author calls "an essentialist notion of the working class"' and read Peronism through Williams's 'structure of feeling' (Bergquist 1990, pp. 309–10); Charles Bergquist warned that Brazilian historians were 'citing and quoting Thompson the way orthodox Marxists used to cite Marx and Lenin' and that 'Thompsonians … might well ponder how to implement his concept of class when so little is known about the class antagonists' (1990, pp. 192, 194). Frederick Cooper's retrospective on Thompson (Social History 1995; unread) preceded his answer to Eley and Nield: 'As in Thompson's England, much of the story is about people struggling not to be a working class'; 'The category-producing class is here to stay. So is the working class' (2000, pp. 62, 67).
strands.works: Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Chandavarkar, The Origins of Industrial Capitalism in India (1994), '"The Making of the Working Class"' (HWJ 43, 1997), Imperial Power and Popular Politics (1998); Viotti da Costa, with Weinstein (ILWCH 36, 1989); James, Resistance and Integration (1988), with French, eds, The Gendered Worlds of Latin American Women Workers (1997), Doña María's Story (2000); Bergquist (1990); Cooper, 'Work, Class and Empire' (1995), Decolonization and African Society (1996), 'Farewell to the Category-Producing Class?' (2000)
